title: Designing Autoscale Rules
description: Scale on the metric that actually predicts load, with cooldowns that stop the fleet oscillating.

data.text: An App Service plan autoscales on CPU above 70%. Every morning at 9 a.m. the fleet scales out to 12 instances, then back to 2 by 9:30, then out again — flapping 40 times a day. On the one genuinely busy day, it never scaled out at all, because CPU stayed at 55% while requests queued for 4 seconds. Redesign the rules.

Scale on a **leading indicator of demand** — request count, queue depth, or concurrent connections — not on a **lagging resource** like CPU. Add a **schedule-based rule** for the predictable morning ramp so you are already at capacity before users arrive, and set **cooldowns** long enough that a scale-out is not immediately followed by a scale-in.

data.title: Profile with schedule floor + metric ramp + cooldowns (Bicep)

data.text: For queue-driven workers the same pattern applies with `ApproximateMessageCount` as the trigger. For AKS, scale on **KEDA** scalers instead of the horizontal pod autoscaler's CPU default, and use the **cluster autoscaler** so node count follows pod count.

CPU rises only once work is already being served, and it can stay moderate while every request waits on a slow database — precisely the day the CPU rule failed to fire. Request and queue metrics measure demand directly, so the fleet grows before users feel it. The long scale-in cooldown addresses the cost side: scaling in too eagerly guarantees you scale out again in ten minutes.

cards.title: Request / queue-depth metric
pros: Predicts load rather than reacting to it
Works for API and worker workloads
cons: Threshold must be tuned per workload
Metric may lag a few minutes

cards.title: Schedule-based scaling
cards.description: Fixed instance count per time window
pros: Zero reaction time for known peaks
cons: Needs maintenance as usage patterns shift
